The handler sends a copied string in a small value and never lets the worker use c.Writer. The channel has a fixed capacity and the process joins its worker. Output order of accepted versus work is intentionally unspecified. This queue is in-memory: returning 202 here does not promise survival of a process crash.

A c.Copy call does not make asynchronous response writes safe or turn the request context into a process context. Unbounded goroutines are an unbounded queue. Sending to a channel while another owner closes it can panic. Test queue-full rejection, shutdown while a handler is enqueueing, duplicate jobs and process recovery separately from ordinary request success.
questions.trap: Copy is not a response-lifetime, goroutine-ownership or durability primitive.
questions.exercise: Replace it with extracted immutable job data, bounded admission and an application-owned worker; define what 202 means after a crash.
questions.solution: The original context is reused and the completed response writer must not be used asynchronously. Copy only helps limited read access and does not deep-copy every referenced value, extend the response or make a job durable. Extract the required input, choose request-bound or separately owned work and define queue capacity and shutdown. For must-complete acceptance, persist the job before responding and make its effect replay-safe.
questions.followUp: Who closes the queue while requests are still attempting to enqueue?

questions.title: A forged forwarded address bypasses a limit
questions.prompt: A service trusts X-Forwarded-For from every peer and rate-limits by c.ClientIP. What can a direct client influence?
answerPoints: A reverse proxy may supply the original client address, but a direct client can also send X-Forwarded-For. If a Go service trusts forwarding headers from every peer, address-based controls can be bypassed. Configure exactly which proxy origins are trusted and make the edge replace or sanitize incoming forwarding headers. An IP address remains a network observation, not a user credential.

Write down the chain of load balancers and ingress proxies. Restrict direct access to the service where practical, configure Gin trust and verify how the edge processes preexisting forwarding headers. Use TLS according to the actual termination boundary. Rate-limit authenticated identities and service capacity as well as addresses; many legitimate users can share one NAT address. With trusted proxies disabled, ClientIP uses the peer address and ignores the claimed forwarded client address. The documentation-only addresses are reserved example ranges. Behind a real controlled proxy, configure its actual narrow address ranges instead of copying these values or trusting all private networks.

Trusting 0.0.0.0/0 or accepting a header called X-User is not authentication. Forwarded host and scheme can also affect generated URLs and redirects. Test a direct spoofed request, a legitimate proxy, multiple forwarded hops and IPv6. Keep proxy configuration immutable while the engine serves traffic and review it after topology changes.
questions.trap: An HTTP header containing an address is not proof that the request passed through a trusted proxy.
questions.exercise: Test a spoofed direct request and a legitimate controlled reverse proxy; identify which layer must sanitize the header chain.
questions.solution: A client can claim arbitrary forwarding information if all peers are trusted. Disable proxy trust when unused or configure narrow controlled proxy origins and edge header processing. Test actual peer versus forwarded hops and IPv6. Address-based controls remain imperfect because legitimate users share NATs and an IP is not an authenticated user; preserve explicit principal/resource authorization and service-capacity limits.
questions.followUp: How do forwarded scheme/host values affect generated links and redirect safety?

questions.title: Recovery middleware versus business rollback
questions.prompt: Recovery catches a panic and returns 500 after a database operation. Which guarantees can you honestly report?
answerPoints: Framework recovery can keep a panic from crashing a request-serving goroutine, but it cannot undo a committed database write or decide whether a remote operation succeeded. Expected application errors should travel through a deliberate mapping policy. Assign one layer to produce the response, and test both its status and public body rather than checking only that the handler returned.

Use table-driven requests with method, path, input, verified identity and expected response. Check status, headers, JSON shape and whether forbidden side effects occurred. Inject a narrow application service and test the real storage adapter separately. Add panic recovery as a last-resort boundary, plus structured logging, without using panic as routine validation control flow. The route records an application error and stops the pending handler chain. After Next returns, middleware maps a known missing value to 404 and writes once if no earlier layer committed the response. The public body is deliberately stable and does not expose a database error. Logging the detailed cause belongs at a protected reporting boundary.

A test that asserts only status 200 can miss a leaked secret body or a second write after an error. Returning an error from a helper does not automatically attach it to Gin. Recovery is not a transaction manager. Test malformed and unauthorized requests, missing resources, dependency cancellation, unknown outcomes and a panic after a simulated effect.
questions.trap: Recovery is not a transaction coordinator and an HTTP error is not evidence of no side effects.
questions.exercise: Write an error-mapping test that checks status, public body and whether the application side effect was already committed.
questions.solution: You can report that the panic was handled at a request boundary, not that storage or external effects were rolled back. Expected errors should have a deliberate mapping and one response writer owner. Test the response body for accidental information exposure and test transaction/effect recovery separately. Neither a nil handler return nor a 500 tells the full business outcome after a partial operation.
questions.followUp: What should the client do after a write timeout whose outcome cannot be determined from the response?

questions.title: Graceful shutdown with workers and WebSockets
questions.prompt: The server calls http.Server.Shutdown and exits as soon as it returns. The application also has workers and hijacked connections. Is shutdown complete?
answerPoints: A router handles requests, while net/http.Server owns listener behavior and connection budgets. A short r.Run example is useful for a tutorial, but a deployed service needs an explicit startup and shutdown owner. Readiness, request admission, long-lived streams, background workers and shared clients must fit the same lifecycle rather than each inventing its own stop signal.

Reject new work during drain and stop reporting readiness before termination when the platform requires it. Allow in-flight operations a defined budget, then join owned workers and close shared dependencies in order. ReadTimeout and WriteTimeout interact with request bodies and streaming, so configure them for the protocol instead of copying one magic timeout to every service. The constructor makes header and idle budgets visible. stop creates a fresh bounded shutdown context rather than using an already-cancelled request context. This example opens no socket. In a native service, separately own Serve or ListenAndServe, distinguish http.ErrServerClosed from a startup failure and decide how to handle shutdown exceeding its budget.

Shutdown does not close or wait for hijacked connections such as custom WebSocket lifetimes. A readiness endpoint that always returns 200 does not prove downstream capacity; avoid making liveness fail merely because a dependency is temporarily unavailable. Test a slow header, cancellation, a long request during drain and a worker that ignores its stop contract in a native integration environment.
questions.trap: A returned Shutdown call is not proof that every resource and background effect is finished.
questions.exercise: Design readiness withdrawal, request drain, worker joining, stream handling and dependency-close order within one termination budget.
questions.solution: Server.Shutdown drains its managed HTTP connections under a context, but does not own every goroutine or wait for hijacked connections. The composition root must separately stop and join workers, manage long-lived connection lifetimes and close shared clients after their borrowers finish. Timeouts depend on the protocol, especially streaming; verify cancellation and test a slow operation during drain.
questions.followUp: How do Kubernetes termination grace and load-balancer propagation affect the available application budget?

questions.title: RPC backend, indexer or blockchain node?
questions.prompt: You need a Go service that reads token balances and indexes events. Does it need to implement consensus or import an entire chain-application framework?
answerPoints: Go is used for blockchain nodes and infrastructure, but a backend that reads balances is not the same system as a validator or a signing service. Start with the target network and the operation you must perform. Prefer the protocol’s maintained libraries, inspect their module boundaries and pin a reviewed release. Adding every blockchain SDK increases dependencies without proving correctness.

For Ethereum applications, use ethclient for typed RPC and accounts/abi or generated bindings for contract encoding; inspect core/types for transactions and receipts. For Bitcoin, distinguish wire/chaincfg from rpcclient and the reviewed btcec, btcutil and txscript module majors. Cosmos SDK builds chain applications and has release-specific compatible modules; it is not a universal Ethereum client. Check the chosen release’s go.mod and official migration guide. The table assigns a role rather than claiming one universal package is best. go-ethereum common/types/abi are subpackages of its module; btcsuite also has separately versioned modules, whose current major path matters. The example is a selection map, not an installation of these libraries or a blockchain runtime in GopherForge.

An SDK’s address parser does not prove a network, token or contract is legitimate. Package APIs, consensus rules, chain IDs and deployed contract ABIs all matter. Pin versions, run dependency verification and vulnerability analysis, and review transitive requirements. Full node, networking, signing and database workflows belong in your native development environment; these readings add no guest sockets, wallet or investment functionality to the app.
questions.trap: A library’s popularity does not make it the right protocol or operational role for every blockchain job.
questions.exercise: Choose package roles for Ethereum RPC/ABI, Bitcoin transaction tooling and an application-specific Cosmos chain, and explain their trust boundaries.
questions.solution: A balance reader and indexer usually need protocol clients, encoding and durable projection logic, not a new consensus implementation. Ethereum ethclient/rpc and abi/types have different roles; Bitcoin and Cosmos ecosystems have their own modules and compatibility rules. Verify network and deployed-contract identity, pin reviewed dependency versions and state the trust placed in RPC providers. The SDK choice does not prove finality, authorization or key security.
questions.followUp: What changes when the job is running a validator or building a new chain application instead?

questions.title: The endpoint is reachable but serves the wrong chain
questions.prompt: The Go client connects successfully to an RPC URL. What must it verify before using balances or preparing transaction intent?
answerPoints: An Ethereum RPC endpoint is an external dependency with latency, availability and trust limits. A successful TCP connection does not prove that the endpoint serves the intended chain or that every call will finish. Use typed clients, time-bounded operations and an expected chain ID configured by the application. Keep node credentials out of logs and never treat RPC data as authenticated business authority by default.

Share an appropriately configured client for its intended lifetime, close it at the owning boundary and pass a fresh operation context to each RPC. Distinguish a transport timeout, JSON-RPC error, missing object and on-chain revert. Read related state at a consistent block/hash where required and report archive/pruning limitations rather than silently substituting latest state. The client calls a local HTTP test server and preserves the JSON-RPC request ID in its reply. The hex result becomes an exact big.Int value. Production code must compare that value with the configured expected chain, rather than accepting any reachable endpoint. A dial context does not become the deadline for every later operation.

Providers can impose batch, rate and historical-range limits. Bound concurrency and response sizes, classify retryable reads and treat a transaction-send timeout as an unknown outcome. A single RPC provider is also a trust and availability assumption. Test wrong chain ID, unavailable history, malformed responses, cancellation and provider disagreement in a local or test-network environment.
questions.trap: Quietly falling back to latest state can turn a reproducible historical query into a different operation.
questions.exercise: Extend the local eth_chainId mock with wrong-chain and timeout responses, and compare dial and per-call context lifetimes.
questions.solution: Compare the reported chain ID with the configured expected identity and give every operation its own budget. A successful dial does not establish network identity or the deadline of subsequent calls. Classify transport, JSON-RPC, missing-data and chain execution outcomes separately. Use a consistent block/hash for related historical reads where required, handle provider pruning/rate limits explicitly and keep endpoint credentials out of logs.
questions.followUp: How would you handle a provider that cannot serve the requested historical block?

questions.title: The token amount lost one base unit
questions.prompt: A decimal token amount is decoded to float64, multiplied by 10^18 and then converted to big.Int. Why can the result already be wrong?
answerPoints: Token amounts frequently exceed the exact integer range of float64, even when the human-readable value looks small. Converting through a float before math/big permanently loses information. Parse text under an explicit decimal-scale policy, reject unsupported precision and preserve the integer base-unit value. Token metadata is input to validate, not an instruction to allocate unbounded memory.

Obtain and verify the correct token contract, network and decimal metadata, then define supported scales and input length. Keep amounts in base units for arithmetic and serialize large integers as exact strings where the wire contract needs them. math/big.Int methods mutate the receiver; use Set for independent copies before sharing values between owners. The sample produces 1000000000000000001 exactly, without a floating-point intermediate. It rejects signs, exponents, excess fractional precision and values outside its stated 256-bit policy. The 36-decimal cap is this example’s application budget, not a claim that every token uses at most that scale.

Symbols are not unique token identifiers, and decimal metadata can be surprising or unsupported. Do not round away an extra fractional digit silently. Test zero, leading zeros, maximum value, too many digits, unsupported scale and the same symbol on different networks. Fees, token transfers and fiat conversions are different quantities with separately defined units and rounding policies.
questions.trap: An exact type at the final step does not repair a lossy intermediate representation.
questions.exercise: Parse 1.000000000000000001 directly under an 18-decimal policy and reject excess precision and out-of-range input.
questions.solution: float64 cannot preserve all relevant integers and decimal fractions, so later converting to big.Int cannot restore lost information. Parse validated decimal text directly to exact base units under an explicit scale, range and rounding policy. Verify the chain, token contract and metadata instead of inferring decimals from a symbol. Bound input size and remember that big.Int methods mutate their receiver when values cross ownership boundaries.
questions.followUp: How should the wire API represent large integers for JavaScript clients without silently losing precision?

questions.title: eth_call succeeded; the transaction still failed
questions.prompt: A contract call simulation succeeds, but a later submitted transaction reverts. Is this necessarily a bug in ABI encoding?
answerPoints: An ABI describes how to encode a call and decode its result. It does not prove that the target address has the expected code or that a read result will remain true in a future transaction. An eth_call evaluates a call against a selected chain state without committing it. State-changing execution requires a separate signed transaction lifecycle and can fail even after a successful simulation.

For reads, use ethclient.CallContract with an explicit block, or an appropriate hash-pinned call when reproducibility requires it. Decode with the same ABI and validate the returned shape. Generated bindings can make the Go surface clearer, but review the generated version and deployed contract compatibility; the newer bind/v2 API is not interchangeable with older binding examples. The example encodes an address into an ABI word without contacting a node or signing anything. HexToAddress is used only after validation, since conversion alone is not an input validator. The encoded bytes must still be paired with a verified chain, contract address and reviewed ABI before a native RPC call.

A method name, ABI file or token symbol does not authenticate deployed code, particularly with upgradeable contracts. A successful simulation is not a promise about inclusion, fees or future state. Test malformed return data, wrong contract/network, a changed implementation, a reverted call and unavailable historical state. Keep signing policy outside a generic ABI helper.
questions.trap: Successful simulation is not authorization or a guarantee of inclusion and successful state change.
questions.exercise: Separate ABI packing, selected-state simulation, transaction construction, inclusion and receipt interpretation; name changes between each stage.
questions.solution: No. The simulation evaluated a selected state without committing it. The later transaction can encounter changed state, nonce, fees, permissions or contract implementation. ABI packing is only encoding, and a generated binding does not authenticate deployed code. Pin the intended chain and contract, decode and validate results, inspect the inclusion receipt and define how reverts and unknown send outcomes are reconciled.
questions.followUp: What is required to make a multi-read historical result reproducible by block hash?

questions.title: Two replicas reserve the same account nonce
questions.prompt: Two Go processes call PendingNonceAt for one account, both receive 42 and prepare different transfers. Would a mutex in each process solve it?
answerPoints: Two Go workers can read the same pending nonce and sign conflicting transactions. A process-local mutex helps only while one process owns the account; it does not coordinate replicas or survive a crash. Give each business intent a stable identity, persist its nonce and signed transaction identity under one ownership protocol, and reconcile unknown send outcomes before allocating new work.

Distinguish prepared, submitted, pending, included, reverted and finalized states. An inclusion receipt with failed status is not a successful business effect. EIP-1559 fee cap, priority fee, gas limit and value have different meanings. A replacement may use the same nonce but a different transaction hash and policy-approved fees; keep the business intent stable and record the replacement chain. Repeating the same business intent reuses its reservation rather than consuming another nonce. The model assumes one owner and intentionally does not persist or sign transactions. A production allocator must atomically store intent and reservation, prevent concurrent owners from diverging and reconcile reservations after restart or account activity outside the service.

A send timeout is not proof that the transaction was rejected. Retrying with a fresh nonce can repeat a transfer; blindly retrying the same underpriced transaction may not solve inclusion. PendingNonceAt is an observation, not a distributed reservation. Test concurrent intents, duplicate requests, external account activity, fee replacement, receipt absence, reorg and restart between signing and send.
questions.trap: A fresh nonce can produce a second business transfer rather than a safe retry of the first.
questions.exercise: Design the durable intent/reservation record, single-account ownership or fencing, replay identity and recovery after a send timeout.
questions.solution: Separate local locks do not coordinate replicas. One durable account-ownership protocol must reserve a nonce with a stable business intent and persist the signed transaction identity before recovery can reconcile it. PendingNonceAt is a provider observation, not a reservation service. Track pending, replacement, included, reverted and finalized outcomes, and do not create a new transfer merely because the first send timed out.
questions.followUp: How do external wallet activity, fee replacement and gaps after a crash affect the allocator?

questions.title: A signing service can sign the wrong valid transaction
questions.prompt: An external signer securely stores the key, but a caller can submit any chain, destination and amount. Is key custody enough?
answerPoints: A signing key is authority, not an ordinary configuration string. An RPC URL, ABI helper or generic retry function should not automatically receive it. Separate construction and policy validation from key custody, bind transactions to the intended chain, and record what was approved without logging private keys or seed material. Read-only blockchain work does not require a signer at all.

Use reviewed protocol signing libraries and choose custody appropriate to the threat model, such as a tightly scoped external signer, keystore or hardware-backed process. Plan key rotation, backup, access control and audit records. Off-chain signed messages need domain separation, intended action, expiry and replay protection too; an address recovered from a signature does not automatically prove authorization for every action. The unsigned intent carries a chain ID, nonce, destination, value and distinct fee fields. Constructing it does not authorize or broadcast anything, and the tiny fee values are illustration only. A signer boundary must validate the actual chain, destination, function arguments, amount and fee ceilings against an explicit policy before signing.

Do not invent cryptographic signing or log seed phrases for debugging. Ethereum’s historical Keccak-256 and standardized SHA3-256 are different functions; substituting one silently changes hashes. Chain-bound transaction signatures do not solve every cross-contract or off-chain replay. Test rejection of wrong chain, modified destination, excessive fees, duplicate intent and an unavailable signer without sending real funds.
questions.trap: A correctly signed transaction can still be the wrong transaction for the business and network.
questions.exercise: Define an intent-validation policy, audit record, chain/domain binding, limits and rejection cases without embedding any production key.
questions.solution: Secure custody reduces key exposure but does not validate business intent. The signer boundary or an equally trusted approval boundary must enforce the intended chain, destination/function, amount, nonce identity and fee ceilings. Off-chain messages also need action/domain, expiry and replay policy. Use reviewed protocol primitives, keep key material out of logs and plan rotation and recovery. Signature recovery alone does not grant permission to every action.
questions.followUp: Which audit fields prove what was approved without exposing the signing key or seed?

questions.title: The indexer reconnects after a reorg
questions.prompt: A WebSocket subscription reconnects after missing several blocks, and a previously credited log now belongs to an orphaned block. How does the indexer recover?
answerPoints: A WebSocket subscription is a live notification channel, not a durable ledger cursor. A process can disconnect, a provider can drop a slow subscriber and a chain can reorganize recently observed blocks. Store a checkpoint that includes chain identity and block hash, backfill a bounded range after reconnect and make the projection’s rollback or rebuild behavior explicit.

Use FilterLogs for bounded backfill and SubscribeFilterLogs for live delivery where supported. Record chain ID, block hash/number, transaction hash and log index as required by the projection. Treat removed logs as a signal to reconcile; reconnect with overlap and deduplicate. Bound queues and scan ranges, and checkpoint only after the corresponding durable effect is safe to replay. The second block at height 11 does not extend the current canonical tip, so the model demands reconciliation. It is not a full fork-choice algorithm. A real indexer locates the common ancestor, reverses or rebuilds affected projection state and checkpoints atomically before continuing along the new canonical branch.

A receipt or one observed block is not universal finality. Finality guarantees and acceptable confirmation policy depend on the network, consensus state and business consequence. Do not permanently credit an irreversible external effect solely from an unfinalized subscription event. Test a missed block, duplicate event, removed log, competing hash at one height, crash during projection update and provider history limits.
questions.trap: Remembering only the last event number or transaction hash loses canonical-chain context and can miss removed events.
questions.exercise: Design the canonical checkpoint, bounded backfill overlap, event identity, reversible projection and finality policy.
questions.solution: A subscription is not a durable cursor. Resume from a persisted chain/block-hash checkpoint, backfill with overlap, deduplicate and detect the canonical ancestor when hashes diverge. Roll back or rebuild affected projection state and checkpoint with its durable effect. Finality and acceptable confirmation policy depend on the network and business risk; an unfinalized observed log must not automatically trigger an irreversible external credit.
questions.followUp: What if the RPC provider has pruned the history required for reconciliation?

questions.title: A valid JWT reaches another user’s object
questions.prompt: Signature verification succeeds, but a request asks for another tenant’s order. What checks are still required?
answerPoints: A signed token can be genuine and still belong to the wrong audience, issuer or operation. Even a fully valid token does not prove that its subject may read a particular order. Treat authentication as construction of a verified principal and authorization as an explicit resource-scoped decision. Fail closed when either contract is missing rather than accepting whatever identity-shaped value a request provides.

With JWT, use a maintained verifier, constrain acceptable algorithms and validate key selection, issuer, audience, expiry and other required claims. Parsing or base64-decoding is not verification. Design key rotation and revocation/session policies. For browser clients, choose cookie/CSRF/CORS rules deliberately; CORS is not an authorization mechanism for non-browser callers. The same subject string in a different tenant is denied. This pure function models authorization after authentication; it deliberately does not parse or verify a JWT. Construct the principal only after the authentication layer validates the chosen credential, and test resource rules independently of token parsing.

Do not trust roles or tenant IDs copied from unverified headers or an unverified token payload. Avoid returning a different secret-laden error body for every verification failure. Test wrong issuer/audience, expired and not-yet-valid credentials, unknown keys, missing required claims and a valid credential attempting another tenant’s resource. These are native service lessons, not registration or accounts added to GopherForge.
questions.trap: Authentication and object-level authorization are separate decisions even when a token contains familiar role names.
questions.exercise: List issuer, audience, time and key-selection checks, then write an independent resource authorization test with two tenants.
questions.solution: Verify the full credential contract, not only its signature, and construct a principal only after those checks pass. Then authorize the specific action on the tenant-scoped resource. Client-provided roles or tenant headers are not authority, and CORS does not protect a server from non-browser requests. Include revocation/rotation policy and consistent failure responses without leaking secrets or object details.
questions.followUp: How should a cached authorized response react to permission revocation?

questions.title: A fast hash is proposed for password storage
questions.prompt: A team wants one SHA-256 helper for password storage, signed messages and encryption. Which requirements are being collapsed?
answerPoints: A fast hash, password hash, MAC, encryption scheme and digital signature answer different questions. A SHA-256 digest does not make a password database resistant to guessing, and encryption without authentication can accept altered ciphertext. Use reviewed libraries and document the purpose, key lifetime, input format and resource budget before selecting a primitive.

Use an appropriate reviewed password KDF such as Argon2id where your policy permits it, with random salt and stored algorithm/version/cost parameters. Benchmark memory and CPU cost under concurrent login load and bound admission; expensive verification is also a denial-of-service surface. For secret encryption prefer a reviewed authenticated construction and a key/nonce management design instead of assembling low-level primitives. The secret key comes from crypto/rand rather than a predictable simulation PRNG. HMAC authenticates these exact bytes and hmac.Equal performs the intended tag comparison. This example has no expiry, replay store or message canonicalization policy, so it is not by itself a complete access-token protocol.

Do not use math/rand for secrets, a fast unsalted digest for password storage, or a plain equality loop for secret MAC tags. Do not copy one parameter value forever from a tutorial. Test corrupted tags, wrong keys, duplicate/replayed messages, unsupported KDF parameters and resource exhaustion. Keep production keys outside code and logs, and define rotation and recovery procedures.
questions.trap: A cryptographic algorithm name is not a complete protocol, storage or resource-management design.
questions.exercise: Assign password KDF, MAC, authenticated encryption and signature roles, then identify randomness, key, replay and admission budgets.
questions.solution: These primitives have different purposes. Password storage needs a reviewed slow, memory-aware KDF policy with salt and stored parameters; a MAC authenticates bytes with a secret key; encryption needs confidentiality and authentication; signatures have a separate trust model. Use crypto/rand for secret material, constant-time tag verification APIs where intended and explicit key lifecycle. Bound expensive password verification under concurrent load and test hostile parameter/input cases.
questions.followUp: How can an expensive password KDF itself become a denial-of-service surface?

questions.title: A public URL redirects into an internal service
questions.prompt: An outbound-fetch endpoint checks https and an allowed initial hostname, then follows redirects and resolves DNS again. What remains unsafe?
answerPoints: A URL supplied by a user can target internal services, metadata endpoints or a different host after redirection. Checking that the string begins with https is insufficient. Prefer a small configured set of upstream services and let user input select a resource within one of them. When arbitrary destinations are a real requirement, enforce address and egress policy at connection time as well as during URL parsing.

Use an owned http.Client with explicit time and response-size budgets. Disable automatic redirects or revalidate every hop under the same policy. Consider userinfo, ports, IP literals, IPv6, alternate encodings and DNS resolution/rebinding. A reviewed dialer or infrastructure egress control must enforce forbidden internal ranges against the actual connection target; validating a hostname once before a later independent DNS lookup is not enough. The attacker-shaped string stays inside a query parameter on the configured example domain. The code does not send a request and does not claim the upstream application is safe from injection. Its narrower guarantee is that this input cannot select the network host or scheme.

A domain allowlist does not protect a compromised allowed service from returning hostile data, and a URL parser does not establish permission. Do not follow a redirect into a forbidden host or log upstream credentials in the URL. Test fixed-destination behavior, hostile resource IDs, redirects, private addresses, changed DNS answers and decompressed response limits in an isolated native environment.
questions.trap: Parsing a URL and seeing https does not prove that the eventual network peer is allowed.
questions.exercise: Explain fixed destinations, per-hop validation, DNS rebinding, actual dial targets, response limits and credential leakage.
questions.solution: The initial URL check is insufficient. Prefer configured destinations with user data encoded only as resource/query values. Revalidate or disallow redirects and enforce forbidden network ranges against the actual connection under a reviewed dial/egress policy. Independent DNS lookups can invalidate an earlier check. Bound operation time and decompressed body size and avoid leaking credentials from URLs or forwarding authentication to an unintended host.
questions.followUp: How do IPv6, alternate ports and proxy routing change the enforcement point?

questions.title: The certificate error is hidden with InsecureSkipVerify
questions.prompt: A development HTTPS request fails verification. A patch sets InsecureSkipVerify and now the request succeeds. What evidence is lost?
answerPoints: A TLS connection can encrypt traffic to the wrong peer if verification is disabled. Certificate chain trust and hostname identity both matter; changing a boolean until a development request succeeds can silently remove production authentication. Use a deliberate trust store, keep the expected server identity tied to the configured destination and handle private development certificates through a separate test trust configuration.

Use current platform Go defaults and the deployment’s reviewed minimum TLS policy. Configure private roots through a controlled CA process and test hostname mismatches, expired certificates and rotation. For mTLS, define both certificate verification and application authorization for the resulting identity. Plan long-lived connection behavior during rotation and shutdown. The httptest client trusts its associated test certificate without setting InsecureSkipVerify. It demonstrates a scoped native test trust relationship, not a reason to ship that test certificate or trust arbitrary self-signed endpoints. The last check inspects this local test connection’s negotiated TLS version; it does not describe a public endpoint’s configuration.

Do not solve certificate failures by setting InsecureSkipVerify or by accepting every certificate in a callback. TLS does not validate a JSON payload, authorize an object or remove SSRF risk. Keep signing keys and token material out of telemetry. Test a wrong hostname, untrusted root, expired certificate, unavailable revocation/rotation dependencies and the operational recovery path.
questions.trap: Making the error disappear does not establish the correct peer or a safe trust policy.
questions.exercise: Use a scoped test/private trust setup and test wrong hostname, unknown root, expiry and certificate rotation.
questions.solution: Disabling verification removes the intended peer-authentication check; encryption alone can still connect to the wrong endpoint. Fix the deliberate trust relationship and expected hostname rather than accepting arbitrary certificates. Keep development test roots separate from production, plan rotation and distinguish TLS identity from application authorization and payload validation. A successful unverified request is not a secure integration test.
questions.followUp: What additional authorization is needed after a valid mTLS certificate identifies a workload?

questions.title: An atomic pointer publishes a mutable map
questions.prompt: A writer atomically stores *Config, then updates Config.Limits while readers use it. Does atomic.Pointer make the map access safe?
answerPoints: An atomic load or store synchronizes an operation on the atomic value. It does not recursively make the object graph immutable or protect a later map mutation. A useful read-mostly pattern builds a complete independent configuration, publishes one pointer and lets readers hold that immutable snapshot. All fields that must agree belong to the same published value.

Choose a mutex when operations update related state together; choose an atomic primitive only for a precisely defined protocol. Atomic types and mutexes must not be copied after first use. If a snapshot contains slices, pointers or nested maps, define deep-enough copying and lifetime rules. Compare this with sync.Map, whose per-operation contracts do not provide a transaction across arbitrary keys. The map is copied before the pointer is stored. Changing the caller’s input afterward does not mutate the published configuration. Readers load one pointer and keep that snapshot, rather than loading separate fields at different times. A production API should avoid exposing a mutable map from the snapshot to callers.

Publishing a pointer and then changing its map races with readers. Two independent atomic fields do not automatically form a consistent pair. Race detection finds executed data races, not every logical ordering error. Test concurrent publication/read behavior and business invariants with native go test -race; the app sandbox does not supply a native race detector.
questions.trap: Atomic access to a pointer does not recursively apply atomicity to the entire object graph.
questions.exercise: Construct a separate snapshot, copy reachable mutable state, publish once and test concurrent reads/publications natively.
questions.solution: Atomic publication protects the pointer protocol, not later mutations of referenced maps or slices. Build a deep-enough independent snapshot and keep its reachable state immutable, or synchronize all accesses with the same lock protocol. Load one snapshot for fields that must agree; two independent atomics do not create a multi-field transaction. Use native race tests and invariant checks, since absence of a reported race does not prove every logical guarantee.
questions.followUp: How should an API return part of the snapshot without giving callers a mutable map alias?

questions.title: A value receiver copies the mutex but shares the map
questions.prompt: A cache struct holds sync.Mutex and map[string]int. Its Put method uses a value receiver and locks c.mu. Why can it still race?
answerPoints: The presence of a mutex in a struct does not prove that every operation locks the same mutex. A value receiver or assignment can copy the lock while retaining a reference to the same map. Likewise, sync.Map protects its own operations but cannot infer an invariant spanning several keys. Define the state that must change together and keep one synchronization owner for that state.

Use RWMutex when measured read contention justifies it; long-held read locks can still delay writers. A mutex protects the whole declared invariant only if every access participates in the same protocol. sync.Map is suited to documented use patterns such as mostly stable keys or disjoint key ownership, not an automatic replacement for a typed map with multi-step business operations. Both methods use pointer receivers so calls share the lock owner. Snapshot returns independent map storage rather than returning Cache by value or exposing the internal map. This example uses simple scalar values; references inside values would need their own ownership or deeper-copy contract.

Do not copy mutex-bearing values after use, embed them into casually copied API results or return internal maps after unlocking. go vet copylocks helps identify copied locks; native race tests exercise actual access paths. A race-free get-then-put can still duplicate a business action. Test lost updates, snapshots, simultaneous misses and compound invariants separately from the absence of a data-race report.
questions.trap: The mere presence of a lock field does not prove that every access uses the same lock.
questions.exercise: Refactor to one stable lock owner, return an independent snapshot and run native copylocks/race checks plus compound-invariant tests.
questions.solution: The receiver copy gets a different mutex but still points to the shared map storage, so callers do not synchronize on one owner. Use pointer receivers and avoid copying lock-bearing values after use. Protect all reads and writes under the declared protocol and copy exported mutable data deliberately. sync.Map is not a transaction across arbitrary keys, and a data-race-free check-then-act can still violate a business invariant.
questions.followUp: When would measured contention justify RWMutex rather than a simple Mutex?

questions.title: Cancellation is the first select case
questions.prompt: Both ctx.Done and a timer/work channel are ready. The cancellation case appears first in source. Must it win?
answerPoints: Timers have both an API contract and version-dependent implementation behavior. Modern Go timer channels avoid the old buffered stale-value behavior under the documented module/runtime conditions, but this does not let several goroutines reset, receive and decide business state without a protocol. Treat a timer as one owner’s scheduling tool and separately define which events may commit work.

For Go 1.23-and-later timer-channel semantics, inspect the module’s go directive and any asynctimerchan compatibility setting when diagnosing old patterns. Do not use len(timer.C) to synchronize. Stop/Reset documentation distinguishes modern guarantees from older drain patterns. A select with several ready cases chooses among them; listing ctx.Done first does not grant cancellation priority. One goroutine creates, resets and receives the timer. No second receiver can consume its event unexpectedly. The example does not infer fairness or a global ordering against cancellation from a timer firing. It is compatible with the modern timer contract used by the course; review the time package documentation when maintaining older modules or runtime compatibility settings.

Repeated time.After in a hot loop allocates timers and is not a substitute for a clear lifecycle. Stopping a timer does not close its channel or prove a worker exited. If cancellation must prevent a side effect, recheck the operation state under the same synchronization that commits the effect. Test ready timer plus cancellation, reset ownership and shutdown without relying on lucky sleeps.
questions.trap: A lucky timer/cancellation test run does not establish a global priority or a commit ordering guarantee.
questions.exercise: Explain select choice, timer version settings, one-owner Stop/Reset and the synchronization needed before committing a side effect.
questions.solution: Select does not grant source-order priority among ready cases. Give the timer a clear owner and check operation state at the commit boundary under the synchronization that protects the effect. Modern Timer Stop/Reset behavior differs from older compatibility modes, so inspect module go version and runtime settings when maintaining old code. Stopping a timer neither closes its channel nor joins a worker; tests need deliberate barriers and boundary cases.
questions.followUp: What can a cancellation recheck guarantee if another goroutine may commit concurrently?

questions.title: Do returned nil but the response is a failure
questions.prompt: An HTTP dependency returns 500 or an indefinitely large body. The Go caller checks only the error from Client.Do. What is missing?
answerPoints: A successful Client.Do means an HTTP response was received, not that the application operation succeeded. An error page can still be a valid response, and a server can keep streaming bytes after the headers arrive. Reuse the client and transport, pass an operation context and bound both elapsed time and bytes consumed. Closing the body is necessary even when status handling returns early.

Validate the configured positive byte limit and keep its arithmetic within range in a real API. Check status before parsing a success DTO, classify retryable failures and make unsafe writes retry only under an idempotency policy. Bound decompressed response bytes too. Reusing a transport enables connection pooling; reading to EOF can help reuse, but do not drain an untrusted infinite body merely to save a connection. The body is limited to the allowed bytes plus one detection byte, so a truncated success cannot be mistaken for a complete valid response. Client.Timeout covers the overall request including body reading; the context can impose an earlier bound. The sample uses only a local test server and returns the explicit oversize error.

Creating a new transport per request loses useful pooling and may waste sockets. Ignoring Close or using an unbounded ReadAll can exhaust memory. A timeout after sending a write leaves an unknown business outcome, even if no response body was received. Test slow headers, slow body, oversize decompressed data, non-2xx responses, redirects and cancellation in your native service.
questions.trap: A successful transport exchange is not a successful or fully bounded business response.
questions.exercise: Add operation time, status handling, a decompressed-byte limit, Close and a retry policy that distinguishes reads from ambiguous writes.
questions.solution: Do can return a non-2xx response with nil transport error. Check the status, bound body consumption and parse only the intended response shape. Always close the body, reuse the owned client/transport and do not drain an infinite hostile body just to preserve a connection. Client and context budgets include different limits that must be designed together. A timed-out write may have succeeded remotely, so retry only under an explicit idempotency/reconciliation contract.
questions.followUp: How do automatic redirects and compression change destination and byte-budget enforcement?

questions.title: Retrying a partially consumed gRPC stream
questions.prompt: A client receives half a stream, loses the connection and retries the method. What needs to be specified beyond generated stubs?
answerPoints: Generated Go stubs remove repetitive transport code, not the need to design a distributed operation. A gRPC method can block, partially stream data, be retried or outlive its caller unless the application defines its lifetime. Treat protobuf fields as a versioned wire contract and the RPC method as a budgeted operation with explicit authorization and failure semantics.

Set or propagate deadlines because an RPC has no useful universal business timeout. Bound stream queues, use backpressure and make one goroutine own each send/receive direction according to the API contract. Verify metadata-based identity at the server rather than treating all metadata as trusted. Pin protoc and its Go plugins so generated code can be reproduced. The cancelled context maps to the protocol’s cancellation status. It is not rewritten as a successful empty result or confused with expiration of a deadline. In a real handler, domain errors need a deliberate status mapping that does not reveal internal credentials or SQL text; the client separately decides whether a retry is semantically safe.

Do not reuse removed protobuf field numbers; reserve them and keep old message fixtures. A cancelled stream can already have produced durable effects or partial results. Retrying a stream or RPC requires an application identity and a resume/deduplication policy. Test old/new clients, missing deadlines, a slow peer, mid-stream failure and shutdown. Native gRPC networking is taught here, not added to the iOS guest runtime.
questions.trap: Repeating a method call is not necessarily a safe continuation of a partially observed operation.
questions.exercise: Define resume identity, partial-result handling, ordering, duplicate detection, deadlines and compatible protobuf evolution.
questions.solution: Generated stubs do not supply business atomicity or resumability. The operation needs an explicit cursor/identity and ordering/deduplication policy, bounded per-direction ownership and a propagated deadline. Classify cancellation, deadline and domain statuses deliberately. Preserve wire compatibility with reserved removed field numbers and old/new fixtures, and pin the generation tools. Test a slow receiver, mid-stream failure, replay and shutdown with the real transport.
questions.followUp: What differs between a read-only paginated stream and a stream that performs durable writes?

questions.title: Out-of-order work and a dangerous offset commit
questions.prompt: A partition consumer finishes offsets 11 and 13 while 12 is still running. It commits resume offset 14. What can happen after restart?
answerPoints: A broker can redeliver messages after a consumer crash or partition reassignment. Processing records concurrently makes offset handling more subtle: finishing a later record does not prove that earlier records are durable. Track completion per partition and advance only across the contiguous successful prefix. The business effect needs its own deduplication or transaction protocol.

Define the key used for partitioning, the scope of ordering and what counts as durable processing. Commit after the required effect, and retain a stable event identity for idempotent storage changes. Bound queued and in-flight records, observe lag and define a poison-record policy. Libraries such as franz-go provide Kafka protocol clients, not a transaction spanning an arbitrary database and external API. Offsets 11 and 13 are complete, but the next safe offset remains 12. Once 12 completes, the contiguous prefix ends before 14, so 14 is the next record to resume. This pure function models commit arithmetic; actual Go clients have specific commit, rebalance and transaction APIs that must be checked for the pinned version.

Committing offset 14 while record 12 is unfinished can lose that work after a crash. Committing too late can cause duplicates, which is safer only when the effect is replay-safe. During rebalance, an old worker can finish after ownership moved; fence or reconcile its business effects and follow the client’s partition-revocation contract. Test out-of-order completion, duplicates, crash, rebalance and broker timeout.
questions.trap: The largest completed offset is not the same as the largest safely committed contiguous prefix.
questions.exercise: Implement contiguous-prefix accounting and explain durable effects, deduplication and rebalance ownership.
questions.solution: The restart can skip unfinished record 12. Advance only after the contiguous durable prefix is complete and use the client’s documented next-offset semantics. A database effect needs atomic deduplication or another replay-safe design; broker transaction features do not atomically cover arbitrary external services. Bound parallel work and queued records, handle poison messages deliberately and fence or reconcile work that outlives partition ownership during rebalance.
questions.followUp: How would a worker that completes after its partition was revoked be prevented from producing a duplicate effect?

questions.title: A quorum slogan is proposed as a correctness proof
questions.prompt: A service counts three acknowledgements from five replicas and claims every read/write is linearizable. What is absent from that argument?
answerPoints: A network partition can prevent replicas from coordinating. Whether a particular operation may proceed depends on the required consistency contract and the available authority, not on whether the service was written in Go or has a cache. Specify which reads may be stale, which writes require a leader or quorum, and what the caller sees when that requirement cannot be met.

State requirements per use case: a cached catalog may tolerate lag, while spending a balance or reserving an account nonce may require serialized authority. Define read-your-writes behavior, version checks and reconciliation for replicas or projections. Distinguish the availability/consistency tradeoff during a partition from ordinary latency and throughput tradeoffs even when the network is healthy. Three acknowledgements meet a simple majority threshold for five configured replicas; two do not. The predicate demonstrates arithmetic only. Real consensus also needs terms, log ordering, membership changes, persistence and safety rules. Counting arbitrary replies does not prove a linearizable write or that a stale leader cannot act.

Do not claim that a system simply chooses any two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance. A timestamp or a mutex in each replica does not establish a global order. A quorum slogan does not replace a protocol or fault test. Demonstrate split connectivity, stale leadership, concurrent writes, membership changes and recovery, then explain the exact guarantee your operation can still make.
questions.trap: Counting arbitrary replies or naming a system CP/AP does not prove the required business consistency.
questions.exercise: Specify leader/term authority, persistence, ordering, membership and recovery for an operation; contrast a stale catalog read with a balance spend.
questions.solution: A majority predicate is arithmetic, not a consensus algorithm or storage contract. The protocol must establish durable ordering, valid authority, membership rules and the exact read guarantee. During a partition, decide which operations refuse service and which may use stale or independently accepted state under a reconciliation policy. CAP is not a free choice of any two product labels, and local mutexes or timestamps do not create a global order.
questions.followUp: How do read-your-writes, stale leaders and membership changes affect the operation’s guarantee?

questions.title: A comparator using <= and an unstable tie break
questions.prompt: A sort comparator returns a.Priority <= b.Priority. Equal-priority items reorder unpredictably. Which contracts must be fixed?
answerPoints: A comparator must establish a strict weak ordering. In particular, an item is not less than itself. Using <= violates this contract for equal keys, and a comparator that depends on changing external state can violate it while sorting. Define all tie semantics before choosing an implementation.

A stable sort preserves input order among items the comparator considers equal; it does not invent a global order for data that arrived nondeterministically. Add an explicit stable secondary key if different processes must produce the same total result from differently ordered inputs.

Sorting mutates the slice being sorted and can affect aliases to its backing storage. Copy deliberately if the caller retains the original order. For floating-point inputs, specify how NaN and signed zero fit the ordering rather than assuming ordinary < comparisons define every desired relation. Test equal keys, empty data, already sorted data and adversarial boundaries.
questions.trap: Stable sorting cannot repair an invalid comparator or make nondeterministic input order a deterministic business tie break.
questions.exercise: Fix the comparator, predict the order of equal-priority jobs and decide whether the input backing array may be mutated.
questions.solution: Compare priority with <, then either use stable sorting to preserve a meaningful existing order or compare an explicit secondary key. Test irreflexivity and consistency over representative triples, not just one happy output. Use the implementation’s documented comparison/move costs and benchmark expensive payload movement if that matters.
questions.followUp: Would the same stable sort produce identical results if each replica initially received equal-priority items in a different order?
questions.complexity: For the documented stable-sort implementation: O(n log n) comparisons and O(n log² n) swaps; comparator cost and payload movement also matter.

questions.title: A shared descendant is not necessarily a directed cycle
questions.prompt: A DFS marks every visited node as a cycle when reached again. Why does it incorrectly reject a DAG with a shared descendant?
answerPoints: Distinguish unvisited, on the current DFS path, and fully processed nodes. An edge to an active gray node is a back edge and proves a directed cycle; an edge to a completed black node can be an ordinary shared descendant.

An explicit stack stores both the node and the next edge to examine, preserving the same enter/exit structure as recursive DFS. It avoids unbounded reliance on the call stack, but still needs an input-size budget and valid vertex indexes. Visit every connected component, not only the first root.

For undirected graphs, a parent edge needs different treatment, and multigraph/self-loop policy must be explicit. Graph mutation during traversal requires ownership or a consistent snapshot. Test empty graphs, isolated vertices, shared descendants, self-loops and a cycle outside the initial component.
questions.trap: One visited bit cannot distinguish a current-path back edge from a previously completed node in a directed graph.
questions.exercise: Trace colors and stack frames for 0→1, 0→2, 1→3, 2→3, then add 3→0 and explain the first cycle-proving edge.
questions.solution: Use three colors and finish a vertex only after all its outgoing edges are processed. Reject invalid edges rather than indexing outside the graph. The iterative frame advances its edge index before descending and marks the vertex black on exit. The shared descendant is already black; an edge to gray is the cycle evidence.
questions.followUp: How would you return a cycle witness, and what additional predecessor state would that require?
questions.complexity: O(V + E) time and O(V) auxiliary state for a fixed adjacency-list graph.

questions.title: Find a linked-list cycle entry with constant extra space
questions.prompt: A list may contain a cycle after a non-cyclic prefix. How do you find its entry rather than merely report that some cycle exists?
answerPoints: Move slow by one link and fast by two while checking both fast and fast.Next before dereferencing. Meeting pointer identity proves a cycle; comparing node values would be incorrect because different nodes may hold equal values.

After a meeting, move one pointer from the head and one from the meeting point by one step. Their next meeting identifies the entry. Explain the relation between the non-cyclic prefix and the distance travelled around the cycle rather than memorizing an unexplained reset.

The algorithm assumes the next pointers do not change during traversal. It does not reclaim memory, synchronize concurrent mutation or solve arbitrary graph cycles. Test nil head, one acyclic node, a self-loop, repeated values and a cycle with a prefix. A visited-node map is a valid alternative when extra memory or a traversal history is useful.
questions.trap: Equal values do not establish node identity, and mutating links while traversing invalidates the fixed-list argument.
questions.exercise: Build nodes 1→2→3→2, trace the two phases and then test a nil list and a self-loop.
questions.solution: The first phase either reaches nil safely or finds a meeting inside the cycle. Reset one pointer to head and advance both by one to locate the entry. Return the actual node pointer, not its potentially repeated value. Preserve the input and document exclusive or immutable access during traversal.
questions.followUp: What changes if the input is an arbitrary directed graph rather than a list with at most one next edge per node?
questions.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space on a fixed singly linked list.

questions.title: Distribute keys without remapping every key on membership change
questions.prompt: A service assigns keys with hash(key) % nodeCount. Adding a node moves many keys. What does rendezvous hashing change, and what does it not solve?
answerPoints: Compute a deterministic score for each key–node pair and choose the highest under an explicit tie rule. Adding or removing a node changes winners only where membership affects the maximum, under the chosen scoring model. Plain modulo routing changes the partition formula for many keys.

Every participant must use the same stable node identity, membership view, hash encoding and weighting policy. Length-prefix or otherwise unambiguously encode the pair, so concatenated strings cannot represent different logical pairs. The example uses unweighted scoring and a deterministic lexical tie break.

Hash-based routing is not replication, durability, consensus or an authentication primitive. Membership changes still need migration, stale-owner handling, retries and capacity policy. Hot keys remain hot. Weighted nodes and adversarial keys need a reviewed extension; do not claim that a particular database protocol uses this exact scheme without checking it.
questions.trap: A stable hash function does not make divergent membership views agree or preserve data during a migration.
questions.exercise: Compare key assignments before and after adding a node, then explain how readers find data while migration is incomplete.
questions.solution: Use a stable pair encoding and choose the greatest score independently of the order nodes were listed, with an explicit tie rule. Keep membership versioned and define how owners transfer data or redirect requests. Measure distribution and hot keys on realistic input; do not present expected balance as a deterministic guarantee for every small key set.
questions.followUp: When would a hash ring or precomputed partition table be preferable to scanning every node per lookup?
questions.complexity: Naive unweighted lookup scores every node: O(N) hash operations per key; O(1) extra space beyond inputs, with hash input length included in cost.

questions.title: A cancellation test passes only when the machine is lucky
questions.prompt: A worker test sleeps 10 ms, cancels and sleeps another 10 ms before checking a flag. How do you make the test prove the intended lifecycle?
answerPoints: Use explicit start and completion handshakes so the test knows which state it reached. Waiting an arbitrary wall-clock duration does not establish that the worker started, observed cancellation or completed its cleanup on a loaded machine.

Cancellation signals a request to stop; receiving a completion signal or joining the goroutine proves the owned worker exited. Keep failure timeouts as backstops for a broken implementation, not as the mechanism that orders the happy path.

Test the contract when work is waiting for input, attempting to publish output and shutting down. A closed start signal can establish one happens-before edge; it does not automatically synchronize every shared variable. Native race detection, deterministic fakes or suitable synctest support answer complementary questions.
questions.trap: A timing-dependent green run does not prove the intended happens-before edges or absence of a goroutine leak.
questions.exercise: Replace sleeps with started and exited channels, and add a bounded failure guard for a worker that ignores cancellation.
questions.solution: The test waits for started, cancels, then waits for exited. Cleanup completes before exited is closed, so the final assertion follows actual completion rather than a guessed delay. Add a timeout only to fail a stuck test. Extend the scenario with blocked output and verify that both producers and consumers have an owned exit path.
questions.followUp: How would a fake clock or testing/synctest change the proof when retry timers are involved?

questions.title: Partial I/O: a short write without an error is not success
questions.prompt: An io.Writer returns n < len(p) and nil. Is the caller allowed to report success, and how does that differ from a Reader returning data with EOF?
answerPoints: The Writer contract requires a non-nil error when fewer than len(p) bytes are accepted. Standard copy helpers can convert a short nil-error result into io.ErrShortWrite. Preserve the accepted byte count; do not silently claim every requested byte reached the destination.

Reader has a different contract: process n > 0 bytes before handling the returned error, including EOF. io.ReadFull distinguishes no available bytes from a partial fixed-size record using EOF versus ErrUnexpectedEOF. Matching method signatures does not make Reader and Writer progress/error semantics symmetric.

A generic I/O loop can still block indefinitely or fail to make progress if the underlying object violates useful progress assumptions. Bound input and elapsed work at the appropriate owner, classify partial side effects and define retry/resume behavior. Test short writes, data-plus-error, empty input and truncated records rather than only bytes.Buffer success.
questions.trap: Ignoring n or treating Reader and Writer error contracts as identical can silently truncate data.
questions.exercise: Run io.Copy against a deliberately broken short writer and explain the returned count and ErrShortWrite; then compare a truncated ReadFull.
questions.solution: The short writer violates its contract. io.Copy or the source’s WriterTo implementation reports the accepted count and a short-write error, so the caller must not mark the full payload delivered. In fixed-size reads, distinguish zero-byte EOF from partial-record ErrUnexpectedEOF and process any received bytes before deciding the recovery policy.
questions.followUp: When is retrying a partially written request unsafe because the remote side may already have applied an effect?
questions.complexity: Well-behaved streaming copy is O(B) byte work with bounded buffers; blocking time and retry semantics depend on the underlying I/O.
